Liquid molecules can move past one another.
Gas molecules move freely throughout their container.
Plasma particles move freely and do not remain at fixed positions.

mcqs.stem: Amount of a substance in terms of numbers is measured in:
rationales: Gram is a unit of mass, not amount of substance.
Kilogram is a unit of mass, not amount of substance.
Newton is a unit of force.
The mole measures amount of substance by counting particles.

mcqs.stem: Which one of the following unit is not a derived unit?
rationales: Pascal is a derived unit of pressure.
Kilogram is an SI base unit, not a derived unit.
Newton is a derived unit of force.
Watt is a derived unit of power.

mcqs.stem: The length of vernier scale is:
rationales: In the standard school vernier caliper, the vernier scale has a length of 9 mm.
10 mm is not the length of the standard vernier scale described here.
2 cm is not the length of the standard vernier scale.
10 cm is not the length of the standard vernier scale.

mcqs.stem: A ball is thrown vertically upward. Its velocity at the highest point is:
rationales: The ball’s velocity is not −10 m s⁻¹ at the highest point; its instantaneous velocity is zero.
At the highest point, the ball momentarily has zero velocity.
10 m s⁻¹ is not its velocity at the highest point.
The correct value is listed: the velocity is zero.

mcqs.stem: The number of forces that can be added by head to tail rule are:
rationales: The rule is not limited to two forces.
Three forces can be added using the rule, but this is not the maximum.
Four forces can be added using the rule, but this is not the maximum.
The head-to-tail rule can add any number of forces.

mcqs.stem: The value of "g" on the surface of moon is:
rationales: 8.87 m s⁻² is not the Moon’s surface gravitational acceleration.
3.7 m s⁻² is approximately the value on Mars.
The Moon’s surface gravitational acceleration is approximately 1.62 m s⁻².
274.2 m s⁻² is not the Moon’s surface gravitational acceleration.

mcqs.stem: The energy stored in a dam is:
rationales: A dam stores water’s energy before it is converted into electrical energy.
Water stored at a height has gravitational potential energy.
Elastic energy is stored in stretched or compressed objects.
Thermal energy is not the principal energy stored in dam water.

mcqs.stem: The density of aluminum is:
rationales: 2500 kg m⁻³ is not the standard approximate density of aluminum.
920 kg m⁻³ is not the standard approximate density of aluminum.
7900 kg m⁻³ is approximately the density of iron, not aluminum.
Aluminum’s density is approximately 2700 kg m⁻³.

mcqs.stem: Density has formula:
rationales: Mass multiplied by volume is not the formula for density.
Volume divided by mass is the reciprocal of density.
Area divided by mass is not the formula for density.
Density equals mass divided by volume.

mcqs.stem: SI unit of acceleration is:
rationales: m s⁻¹ is the unit of velocity.
m s⁻² is the SI unit of acceleration.
m²s is not the SI unit of acceleration.
m s² is not the SI unit of acceleration.

mcqs.stem: Torque τ is equal to:
rationales: F × m is ambiguous and is not the standard torque formula as written.
F × R² has incorrect dimensions for torque.
F × t does not give torque.
Torque equals force multiplied by the perpendicular lever arm, denoted here by L.

mcqs.stem: If the velocity of a body becomes double, then its kinetic energy:
rationales: Kinetic energy does not remain unchanged when velocity doubles.
Since kinetic energy is proportional to velocity squared, it does not merely double.
Because K = ½mv², doubling velocity makes kinetic energy four times as large.
Doubling velocity does not halve kinetic energy.

mcqs.stem: The energy of a moving body during motion is called:
rationales: Nuclear energy is stored in atomic nuclei, not the energy of ordinary motion.
Chemical energy is stored in chemical bonds, not the energy of motion.
The energy a body has because it is moving is kinetic energy.
Potential energy is associated with position or configuration, not motion.

mcqs.stem: The interval of 200 μs is equivalent to:
rationales: 200 μs equals 0.0002 s, not 0.2 s.
200 μs equals 0.0002 s, not 0.02 s.
Since 1 μs = 10⁻⁶ s, 200 μs = 2 × 10⁻⁴ s.
2 × 10⁻⁶ s is only 2 μs, not 200 μs.

mcqs.stem: A body satisfies second condition of equilibrium if:
rationales: ∑Fₓ = 0 is only the horizontal force-balance condition.
∑Fᵧ = 0 is only the vertical force-balance condition.
∑F = 0 is the first condition of equilibrium, not the second.
The second condition of equilibrium is that the net torque is zero.

mcqs.stem: The unit of energy is:
rationales: Watt is the unit of power, not energy.
Joule is the SI unit of energy.
Newton is the unit of force, not energy.
Mole is the unit of amount of substance, not energy.

mcqs.stem: One pascal is equal to:
rationales: One pascal is one newton per square metre, or 1 N m⁻².
10⁴ N m⁻² is not equal to one pascal.
10² N m⁻² is not equal to one pascal.
10³ N m⁻² is not equal to one pascal.

mcqs.stem: A body is in equilibrium when its
rationales: Uniform acceleration can be nonzero, so this alone does not mean equilibrium.
Uniform speed alone does not rule out changing direction and acceleration.
Uniform speed and uniform acceleration do not necessarily imply equilibrium.
In equilibrium the resultant force and hence the acceleration are zero.

mcqs.stem: If the velocity of a body becomes double, then its kinetic energy will
rationales: Kinetic energy changes when velocity doubles.
Kinetic energy becomes four times, not merely double.
Because K = ½mv², doubling velocity makes kinetic energy four times as large.
Doubling velocity does not halve kinetic energy.

mcqs.stem: Rate of doing work is called.
rationales: Energy is the capacity to do work, not the rate of doing it.
Torque is the turning effect of a force.
Momentum is the product of mass and velocity.
Power is the rate of doing work.

mcqs.stem: Which one of the following is a vector quantity?
rationales: Speed has magnitude only and is a scalar.
Distance has magnitude only and is a scalar.
Mass has magnitude only and is a scalar.
Force has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector.

mcqs.stem: Rate of change of momentum is equal to
rationales: Torque describes rotational effect, not rate of change of momentum.
By Newton’s second law, force equals the rate of change of momentum.
Distance is a measure of separation, not rate of change of momentum.
Mass is a property of matter, not rate of change of momentum.

mcqs.stem: The turning effect of force is called.
rationales: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity.
The turning effect of a force is called torque.
Pressure is force per unit area.
Work is done when a force causes displacement.

mcqs.stem: The centripetal force is inversely proportional to
rationales: Centripetal force is directly proportional to mass when other quantities are fixed.
Centripetal force is proportional to the square of velocity, not inversely to velocity.
From F = mv²/r, centripetal force is inversely proportional to radius.
Centripetal force is directly proportional to the square of velocity.

mcqs.stem: The work will be zero when angle between force and displacement is
rationales: At 45°, the force has a nonzero component along the displacement, so work is nonzero.
At 60°, the force has a nonzero component along the displacement, so work is nonzero.
At 180°, the work is negative but not zero.
Work is zero at 90° because the force is perpendicular to the displacement.

mcqs.stem: The force exerted perpendicularly on unit area of an object is called.
rationales: Strain is the fractional change in dimension of an object.
Young’s modulus is the ratio of stress to strain.
Pressure is force acting perpendicularly per unit area.
Buoyant force is the upward force exerted by a fluid.

mcqs.stem: If “m” is the mass of a body and “c” is its specific heat, then its heat capacity is given by
rationales: Heat capacity is not mass divided by specific heat.
Heat capacity is not specific heat divided by mass.
Heat capacity equals mass multiplied by specific heat, C = mc.
The expression mc² is not the formula for heat capacity.

mcqs.stem: One horse power is equal to:
rationales: 764 W is not the standard value of one horsepower.
One horsepower is approximately 746 W.
674 W is not the standard value of one horsepower.
647 W is not the standard value of one horsepower.

mcqs.stem: In SI, the unit of density is:
rationales: kg m⁻¹ is not the SI unit of density.
kg m⁻² is not the SI unit of density.
Density is mass per volume, so its SI unit is kg m⁻³.
kg m is not the SI unit of density.

mcqs.stem: Equation of momentum is:
rationales: Momentum is not velocity divided by mass.
Momentum is not mass multiplied by velocity squared.
Momentum is not the square of mass times velocity.
Momentum equals mass multiplied by velocity, p = mv.

mcqs.stem: A force “F” acting along x-axis, its y-component is:
rationales: A force entirely along the x-axis has zero y-component.
F is the force’s x-component, not its y-component.
1 is not the y-component of the force.
2F is not the y-component of the force.

mcqs.stem: Which one of the given units is not a derived unit?
rationales: Watt is a derived SI unit of power.
Newton is a derived SI unit of force.
Pascal is a derived SI unit of pressure.
Kilogram is an SI base unit, not a derived unit.

mcqs.stem: The ability of a body to do work is called:
rationales: Power is the rate at which work is done.
Energy is the capacity or ability to do work.
Force is an interaction that can change motion, not the ability to do work.
Pressure is force per unit area.

mcqs.stem: A force acting along x-axis, its y-component is:
rationales: A force along the x-axis has zero y-component.
1 is not the y-component of the force.
F is the force’s x-component, not its y-component.
2F is not the y-component of the force.

mcqs.stem: A car having mass 400kg moving with velocity 2ms⁻¹. Its kinetic energy will be:
rationales: The kinetic energy is not 100 J.
The kinetic energy is not 200 J.
Kinetic energy is ½mv² = ½ × 400 × 2² = 800 J.
The kinetic energy is not 1600 J.

mcqs.stem: The SI unit of pressure is Pascal, which is equal to:
rationales: One pascal equals one newton per square metre, or 1 N m⁻².
10 N m⁻² is ten pascals, not one pascal.
10² N m⁻² is one hundred pascals, not one pascal.
10³ N m⁻² is one thousand pascals, not one pascal.

mcqs.stem: An interval of 200 μs is equal to:
rationales: 0.2 s is 200,000 μs, not 200 μs.
0.02 s is 20,000 μs, not 200 μs.
2 × 10⁻⁶ s equals 2 μs, not 200 μs.

mcqs.stem: Third equation of motion is:
rationales: S = vt is not the third equation of motion in general.
The third equation of motion is v_f² − v_i² = 2aS.
v_f = v_i + at is the first equation of motion.
F = ma is Newton’s second law, not an equation of motion.

mcqs.stem: Coefficient of friction between tyre and dry road is:
rationales: The textbook value for the coefficient of friction between a tyre and a dry road is approximately 1.
0.1 is too small for the stated textbook value.
2 is not the stated textbook value for a tyre on a dry road.
0.2 is too small for the stated textbook value.

mcqs.stem: Centripetal force (F_c) is equal to:
rationales: mv²/r² has an extra factor of 1/r.
mv/r² does not have the dimensions of force.
mv/r is not the formula for centripetal force.
Centripetal force is F_c = mv²/r.

mcqs.stem: SI unit of power is:
rationales: m s⁻¹ is a unit of speed, not power.
A second is a unit of time.
m s⁻² is a unit of acceleration.
The watt is the SI unit of power.

mcqs.stem: Identify the Base Quantity
rationales: Speed is a derived quantity, equal to distance divided by time.
Area is a derived quantity, equal to length squared.
Force is a derived quantity, measured in newtons.
Distance represents length, which is a base quantity.

mcqs.stem: States of Equilibrium are:
rationales: There are not four standard states of equilibrium.
The three states are stable, unstable, and neutral equilibrium.
There are three states of equilibrium, not two.
There is more than one state of equilibrium.

mcqs.stem: Inertia depends upon:
rationales: Inertia depends on mass: greater mass means greater inertia.
Force can change motion but does not determine an object's inertia.
Velocity does not determine inertia.
Acceleration does not determine inertia.

mcqs.stem: Centripetal Force is Directly Proportional to:
rationales: Centripetal force is proportional to mass, not to mass squared.
From F = mv²/r, centripetal force is directly proportional to v² when mass and radius are fixed.
Centripetal force is proportional to the square of speed, not speed alone.
Centripetal force is inversely proportional to radius, not directly proportional to it.

mcqs.stem: In S.I. Unit of Pressure is Pascal which is equal to:
rationales: A pascal is one newton per square metre, or N m⁻².
N m⁻¹ is not the unit equivalent to a pascal.
N m is a unit of work or energy, not pressure.
N m⁻³ is not the unit equivalent to a pascal.

mcqs.stem: The least count of Vernier Calliper is:
rationales: 0.01 mm is not the usual least count of a standard school Vernier caliper.
A standard school Vernier caliper commonly has a least count of 0.01 cm, or 0.1 mm.
1 mm is larger than the usual least count of a Vernier caliper.
1 cm is far too large to be the least count of a Vernier caliper.

mcqs.stem: An example of Neutral Equilibrium is:
rationales: A football lying on a level surface can be an example of neutral equilibrium because a small displacement does not change its height.
A block is not the standard example of neutral equilibrium in this set.
A pencil balanced on its tip is an example of unstable equilibrium.
A book resting on a table is an example of stable equilibrium.

mcqs.stem: The Least Count of Digital Vernier Callipers is:
rationales: A digital Vernier caliper commonly has a resolution of 0.01 mm.
0.1 mm is a coarser resolution than the usual digital Vernier caliper least count.
0.1 cm equals 1 mm, which is too coarse for the usual digital Vernier caliper.
0.01 cm equals 0.1 mm, not the usual 0.01 mm resolution.

mcqs.stem: Newton's First Law of Motion is valid only in the absence of:
rationales: The law does not require the absence of all forces; forces may act and balance.
Newton's first law describes motion when the net force is zero.
Torque is not the condition stated by Newton's first law.
Momentum need not be absent; it remains constant when the net force is zero.

mcqs.stem: Conversion of 72 kmh⁻¹ to ms⁻¹ is equal to:
rationales: 72 km h⁻¹ converts to 20 m s⁻¹, not 10 m s⁻¹.
25 m s⁻¹ is not the result of the conversion.
30 m s⁻¹ is not the result of the conversion.

mcqs.stem: The number of Perpendicular Components of a Force is:
rationales: A force resolved into perpendicular components has two components.
A force in a plane is resolved into two mutually perpendicular components.
Four components are not needed for the standard perpendicular resolution of a force.
Five components are not needed for the standard perpendicular resolution of a force.

mcqs.stem: The value of ‘g’ on the surface of Sun is:
rationales: 1.62 m s⁻² is approximately the gravitational acceleration on the Moon.
3.7 m s⁻² is approximately the gravitational acceleration on Mars.
The Sun's surface gravitational acceleration is approximately 274.2 m s⁻².
8.87 m s⁻² is approximately the gravitational acceleration on Venus.

mcqs.stem: 5 Litre is equal to:
rationales: Since 1 L = 10⁻³ m³, 5 L = 5 × 10⁻³ m³.
5 × 10³ m³ is much larger than 5 L.
5 × 10² m³ is much larger than 5 L.
5 × 10⁻² m³ equals 50 L, not 5 L.

mcqs.stem: Which one of the following is not a derived unit?
rationales: Pascal is a derived unit of pressure.
Kilogramme is an SI base unit, not a derived unit.
Newton is a derived unit of force.
Watt is a derived unit of power.

mcqs.stem: The spinning motion of a body about its axis is called?
rationales: Rotatory motion is the spinning of a body about its axis.
Vibratory motion is repeated back-and-forth motion.
Circular motion is motion along a circular path, not necessarily spinning about the body's own axis.
Random motion has no fixed path or direction.

mcqs.stem: Which one of the following is a vector quantity?
rationales: Distance is a scalar quantity.
Weight is a force and therefore a vector quantity.
Mass is a scalar quantity.
Speed is a scalar quantity.

mcqs.stem: The product of force and displacement is called
rationales: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
Momentum is the product of mass and velocity.
Power is the rate of doing work.
Work is the product of force and displacement in the direction of the force.

mcqs.stem: Racing Cars are made stable by.
rationales: Increasing speed does not by itself make a racing car more stable.
Decreasing mass alone does not ensure greater stability.
Decreasing width can make a car less stable.
Lowering the centre of gravity increases stability.

mcqs.stem: The density of a substance can be found with the help of.
rationales: Pascal’s law describes pressure transmission in a fluid, not how to determine density.
Hooke’s law relates force to extension within the elastic limit.
The principle of floatation concerns the weight of a floating body and displaced fluid.
Archimedes’ principle can be used to determine a substance’s density from its upthrust.

mcqs.stem: SI unit of pressure is Pascal, which is equal to.
rationales: 10⁴ N m⁻² is not equal to one pascal.
10³ N m⁻² is not equal to one pascal.
10⁻² N m⁻² is less than one pascal.
One pascal equals 1 N m⁻².

mcqs.stem: Normal temperature of human body is.
rationales: 15 °C is below normal human body temperature.
37 °F is far below normal human body temperature.
98.8 °C is dangerously high and not normal body temperature.
Normal human body temperature is approximately 37 °C.

mcqs.stem: Least count of vernier callipers is.
rationales: 0.01 mm is not the standard least count for the usual school vernier callipers.
The usual school vernier callipers have a least count of 0.01 cm, or 0.1 mm.
1 mm is too large for the usual vernier callipers' least count.
1 cm is far too large for the least count.

mcqs.stem: The branch of Physics which study the internal structure of the earth is called.
rationales: Geophysics studies the physical structure and properties of the Earth.
Light is a topic in optics, not the study of Earth's internal structure.
Atomic physics studies atoms and their constituents.
Heat is a topic concerning thermal energy, not Earth's internal structure.

mcqs.stem: The rate of change of displacement of a body is called.
rationales: Speed is the rate of change of distance.
Velocity is the rate of change of displacement.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
Deceleration is negative acceleration or a decrease in velocity.

mcqs.stem: The unit of force is.
rationales: The newton is the SI unit of force.
The pascal is the SI unit of pressure.
The joule is the SI unit of energy and work.
The kilogram is the SI unit of mass.

mcqs.stem: The turning effect of a force is called.
rationales: Torque is the turning effect of a force.
Momentum is the product of mass and velocity.
Pressure is force per unit area.
Force is the cause of the turning effect, not its name.

mcqs.stem: The value of “g” on the surface of moon is.
rationales: The acceleration due to gravity at the Moon’s surface is about 1.62 m s⁻².
10 m s⁻² is approximately Earth's gravitational acceleration, not the Moon's.
9.8 m s⁻² is Earth's approximate gravitational acceleration.
20 m s⁻² is not the Moon’s surface gravitational acceleration.

mcqs.stem: The energy stored in dam water is.
rationales: Water stored in a dam does not primarily store electric energy.
Dam water stores gravitational potential energy because it is elevated.
Kinetic energy is associated with motion, not water at rest in a dam.
Thermal energy is not the main form of energy stored in dam water.

mcqs.stem: Potential energy (P.E.) =:
rationales: Incorrect: potential energy is not weight multiplied by acceleration due to gravity.
Incorrect: weight multiplied by mass is not gravitational potential energy.
Incorrect: this omits the object's weight or mass.
Correct: gravitational potential energy is weight multiplied by height, P.E. = wh.

mcqs.stem: According to Pascal's law, F₂ = ____
rationales: Correct: Pascal's law gives F₂/A = F₁/a, so F₂ = F₁A/a.
Incorrect: this reverses the piston-area ratio.
Incorrect: this does not give the force relation from Pascal's law.
Incorrect: this does not give the force relation from Pascal's law.

mcqs.stem: 50°C is equal to:
rationales: Incorrect: 100°F is about 37.8°C.
Correct: 50°C converts to 122°F.
Incorrect: 133°F is about 56.1°C.
Incorrect: 140°F is 60°C.

mcqs.stem: A measuring cylinder is used to measure:
rationales: Incorrect: a measuring cylinder does not measure mass.
Incorrect: a measuring cylinder does not measure area.
Correct: a measuring cylinder is used to measure liquid volume.
Incorrect: it may show a liquid's level, but its stated purpose is measuring volume.

mcqs.stem: Which is a derived unit?
rationales: Correct: the newton is a derived SI unit, equivalent to kg·m·s⁻².
Incorrect: the mole is an SI base unit.
Incorrect: the meter is an SI base unit.
Incorrect: the second is an SI base unit.

mcqs.stem: A ball thrown vertically upward, its velocity at the highest point is:
rationales: Incorrect: at the highest point, the ball's instantaneous velocity is zero.
Correct: the ball momentarily has zero velocity at its highest point.
Incorrect: the ball is not moving upward at 10 m s⁻¹ at the highest point.
Incorrect: −10 m s⁻¹ is not the velocity at the highest point.

mcqs.stem: Centripetal force (F꜀) is equal to:
rationales: Incorrect: the formula has an extra factor of r in the denominator.
Incorrect: this omits one factor of velocity and has the wrong denominator.
Incorrect: this omits one factor of velocity.
Correct: centripetal force is F꜀ = mv²/r.

mcqs.stem: Value of Cos60° is:
rationales: Correct: cos 60° equals 0.5.
Incorrect: cos 60° is not 0.6.
Incorrect: 0.707 is approximately cos 45°.
Incorrect: 0.866 is approximately cos 30°.

mcqs.stem: The first condition of equilibrium is:
rationales: Incorrect: Στ = 0 is the second condition of equilibrium.
Incorrect: this states the second condition, not the first.
Correct: the first condition requires the net force to be zero.
Incorrect: Σw = 0 is not the general first condition of equilibrium.

mcqs.stem: Which is SI unit of acceleration?
rationales: Incorrect: ms is not the SI unit of acceleration.
Correct: acceleration is measured in metres per second squared, m s⁻².
Incorrect: m s⁻¹ is the unit of velocity.
Incorrect: m²s is not the SI unit of acceleration.

mcqs.stem: Second condition of equilibrium is:
rationales: Incorrect: ΣF = 0 is the first condition of equilibrium.
Correct: the second condition requires the net torque to be zero.
Incorrect: ΣN = 0 is not the second condition of equilibrium.
Incorrect: ΣG = 0 is not the second condition of equilibrium.

mcqs.stem: Energy stored in the stretched bow is called:
rationales: Incorrect: a stretched bow stores energy rather than having energy of motion.
Incorrect: this is a broad category, but the specific stored energy is elastic potential energy.
Incorrect: mechanical energy is the total of kinetic and potential energy, not the specific type asked for.
Correct: the stretched bow stores elastic potential energy.

mcqs.stem: SI unit of stress is:
rationales: Incorrect: the newton is a unit of force, not stress.
Correct: stress is force per unit area, measured in N m⁻².
Incorrect: N m² is not the unit of stress.
Incorrect: N m⁻¹ is not the unit of stress.

mcqs.stem: The least count of meter rod is ______.
rationales: Correct: a standard meter rod has a least count of 1 mm.
Incorrect: 0.01 m is 1 cm, not the least count.
Incorrect: 0.01 cm is 0.1 mm, smaller than the meter rod’s least count.
Incorrect: 0.01 mm is much smaller than the meter rod’s least count.

mcqs.stem: Prefix femto is equal to ______.
rationales: Incorrect: 10⁻⁹ is the prefix nano.
Incorrect: 10⁻¹² is the prefix pico.
Correct: femto represents 10⁻¹⁵.
Incorrect: 10⁻¹⁸ is the prefix atto.

mcqs.stem: Co-efficient of friction is equal to ______.
rationales: Incorrect: the coefficient of friction is not the product of frictional force and reaction.
Incorrect: this is the reciprocal of the coefficient of friction.
Incorrect: the coefficient is not the sum of these forces.
Correct: coefficient of friction equals frictional force divided by normal reaction, μ = Fₛ/R.

mcqs.stem: ______ vectors can be added by head to tail rule.
rationales: Correct: the head-to-tail rule can be used to add any number of vectors.
Incorrect: the rule is not limited to exactly four vectors.
Incorrect: the rule is not limited to exactly three vectors.
Incorrect: the rule is not limited to exactly two vectors.

mcqs.stem: The work done will be zero when the angle between the force and the displacement is ______.
rationales: Incorrect: at 45°, the force has a component along the displacement, so work is nonzero.
Incorrect: at 60°, the force has a component along the displacement, so work is nonzero.
Correct: work is zero when force and displacement are perpendicular, at 90°.
Incorrect: at 180°, the work is negative, not zero.

mcqs.stem: ______ (metal) is the lightest.
rationales: Incorrect: copper is denser than aluminium.
Correct: aluminium is the lightest metal among these choices.
Incorrect: mercury is a very dense liquid metal.
Incorrect: lead is a very dense metal.

mcqs.stem: The major source of heat energy is ______.
rationales: Correct: the Sun is Earth’s major source of heat energy.
Incorrect: the Moon reflects sunlight and is not a major heat source.
Incorrect: Earth contains internal heat, but it is not the major source of heat energy for us.
Incorrect: light is a form of energy, not the major source named here.

mcqs.stem: The efficiency of an electric lamp is ______ percent.
rationales: Incorrect: a conventional electric lamp’s efficiency is not typically 20%.
Incorrect: a conventional electric lamp’s efficiency is not typically 15%.
Incorrect: a conventional electric lamp’s efficiency is not typically 10%.
Correct: the textbook value for an electric lamp’s efficiency is about 5%.

mcqs.stem: The weight of a body is 147 N, its mass will be ______ (if g = 10 ms⁻²).
rationales: Incorrect: 1.47 kg would have a weight of 14.7 N at the given g.
Correct: mass = weight/g = 147/10 = 14.7 kg.
Incorrect: 0.147 kg would have a weight of 1.47 N.
Incorrect: 147 kg would have a weight of 1470 N.

mcqs.stem: If velocity of a body becomes three times greater, then kinetic energy will be ______ times.
rationales: Incorrect: kinetic energy is proportional to the square of velocity, not velocity itself.
Incorrect: tripling velocity does not make kinetic energy four times as large.
Incorrect: tripling velocity does not make kinetic energy six times as large.
Correct: KE ∝ v², so tripling velocity makes kinetic energy 3² = 9 times as large.

mcqs.stem: Co-efficient of friction between tyre and dry road is ______.
rationales: Incorrect: 0.1 is too low for the stated tyre–dry-road value.
Incorrect: 0.2 is too low for the stated tyre–dry-road value.
Incorrect: 2 is not the expected coefficient for this textbook example.
Correct: the textbook value for friction between a tyre and a dry road is 1.

mcqs.stem: 1 km h⁻¹ is equal to ______.
rationales: Correct: 1 km h⁻¹ = 1000/3600 m s⁻¹ = 10/36 m s⁻¹.
Incorrect: 36/10 m s⁻¹ is the reciprocal conversion factor.
Incorrect: 1 km h⁻¹ is much less than 10 m s⁻¹.
Incorrect: 36 m s⁻¹ is far too large for 1 km h⁻¹.

mcqs.stem: A force F⃗ is acting along x-axis, its y-component will be ______.
rationales: Incorrect: a force along the x-axis has no y-component of 2F.
Incorrect: a force along the x-axis has no y-component of F.
Incorrect: 1 is not a force component and is not the y-component here.
Correct: a force along the x-axis has zero y-component.

written.text: State Law of Conservation of Momentum. Explain it with Balls Example.
modelAnswer: The total momentum of an isolated system remains constant, provided no external force acts on it.
Thus, total momentum before interaction = total momentum after interaction.
For two balls of masses m₁ and m₂, with initial velocities u₁ and u₂ and final velocities v₁ and v₂:
m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
When two balls collide, one ball may lose momentum while the other gains it; the total momentum of both balls remains unchanged.

rubric.why: The example illustrates that momentum transferred between the balls does not change their combined momentum.
rubric.description: Explains how the collision demonstrates conservation.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that the momentum lost by one ball is gained by the other, so their total momentum remains unchanged.

written.text: The head of a nail is a square of side 10 mm. Find the pressure on it due to a Force of 20 N.
modelAnswer: Given: F = 20 N, side = 10 mm = 0.01 m.

Pressure = 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

written.text: A cyclist completes half round of a circular track of radius 318 m in 1.5 minutes. Find its speed and velocity.
modelAnswer: Given: radius r = 318 m; time t = 1.5 min = 90 s.
Distance travelled in half a round = πr = 3.14 × 318 m = 998.52 m.
Speed = distance ÷ time = 998.52 m ÷ 90 s = 11.1 m/s.
Displacement = diameter = 2r = 2 × 318 m = 636 m.
Average velocity = displacement ÷ time = 636 m ÷ 90 s = 7.07 m/s, along the diameter towards the opposite point.
Speed = 11.1 m/s; average velocity = 7.07 m/s along the diameter.
Speed is the distance travelled per unit time; average velocity is the displacement per unit time in the displacement’s direction.

written.text: A cube of glass of 5 cm side and mass 306 g has a cavity inside it. If the density of glass is 2.55 g cm⁻³, find the volume of the cavity.

Volume of cube = side³ = (0.05 m)³ = 0.000125 m³.
Volume of glass = mass ÷ density = 0.306 kg ÷ 2550 kg m⁻³ = 0.00012 m³.
Volume of cavity = volume of cube − volume of glass = 0.000125 m³ − 0.00012 m³.
Volume of cavity = 0.000005 m³.

written.text: A nut has been tightened by a force of 200 N using 10 cm long spanner. What length of spanner is required to loosen the same nut with 150 N force?

written.text: Derive third equation of motion with the help of graph.
modelAnswer: Draw a velocity-time graph with time on the horizontal axis, velocity on the vertical axis, and a straight line from velocity u at time 0 to velocity v at time t.
The displacement s is the area under the velocity-time graph, which is a trapezium.
Area of trapezium: s = 1/2 (u + v)t
Acceleration: a = (v − u)/t, so t = (v − u)/a
Substitute for t: s = 1/2 (u + v)(v − u)/a
Multiply by 2a: 2as = (u + v)(v − u)
Use the difference of squares: 2as = v² − u²
Therefore, v² = u² + 2as

written.text: A cricket ball is hit vertically upwards and returns to ground 6 S later. Calculate (i) Maximum height reached by the ball. (ii) Initial velocity of the ball

At maximum height, final velocity v = 0.

Maximum height: h = ut − ½gt² = (30)(3) − ½(10)(3²) = 45 m.

written.text: Derive third equation of motion with the help of speed-time graph.
modelAnswer: Let the initial speed be u, the final speed be v, the time be t, the acceleration be a, and the displacement be s.

From the first equation of motion, v = u + at, so t = (v − u)/a.
Substitute for t: s = 1/2(u + v)(v − u)/a = (v² − u²)/(2a).
Therefore, 2as = (u + v)(v − u) = v² − u².
Hence, v² = u² + 2as.

written.text: An object has weight 18 N in air. Its weight is found to be 11.4 N when immersed in water. Calculate its density. Can you guess the material of the object?

Loss of weight in water = 18 N - 11.4 N = 6.6 N.
Formula: relative density = weight in air / loss of weight in water.
Relative density = 18 N / 6.6 N = 2.73.
Formula: density of object = relative density × density of water.

written.text: How can you relate a force with the change of momentum of a body and prove that: (P_f − P_i)/t = F

Since P_i = mu and P_f = mv, F = (mv − mu)/t = (P_f − P_i)/t.

written.text: State and explain the Law of Conservation of momentum with the help of spheres experiment.
modelAnswer: Law: When no net external force acts on a system, its total momentum remains constant.
Take two spheres on a smooth horizontal surface: sphere 1 moves with velocity u1 and sphere 2 is initially at rest (u2 = 0).
They collide and then move with velocities v1 and v2.
Before collision, total momentum = m1u1 + m2u2; after collision, total momentum = m1v1 + m2v2.
Therefore, m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2: the momentum lost by one sphere is gained by the other, and total momentum is conserved.

written.text: Derived the Second Equation of Motion with the help of speed-time graph?
modelAnswer: Displacement s is the area under the speed-time graph.
The area is that of a trapezium: s = 1/2(u + v)t.
From the first equation of motion, v = u + at, so t = (v − u)/a.
Substituting for v in s = 1/2(u + v)t gives s = 1/2(u + u + at)t.
Therefore, s = ut + 1/2at^2, the second equation of motion.

written.text: Determine a force from its perpendicular components.
modelAnswer: Let the perpendicular force components be Fx and Fy.
The resultant force R is the diagonal of the right-angled triangle formed by the components.
By Pythagoras' theorem, R^2 = Fx^2 + Fy^2.
Therefore, the magnitude is R = sqrt(Fx^2 + Fy^2).
If θ is measured from Fx, its direction is given by tan θ = Fy/Fx, so θ = tan^-1(Fy/Fx).

written.text: Define Kinetic energy and derive its formula. KE = 1/2 mv²

Therefore, KE = W = Fs = (ma)(v² / 2a) = ½mv².

written.text: Prove that the rate of change of momentum of a body is equal to a force acting on it.

Since a = (v − u)/t, the rate of change of momentum = ma.
By Newton’s second law, F = ma; therefore, the rate of change of momentum = F.

written.text: Find a force from its perpendicular components by using a figure.

Figure construction: draw OX horizontally to represent Fx and OY vertically to represent Fy; mark angle XOY = 90°.
Choose the scale 1 cm represents 1 N; draw OX to length Fx cm and OY to length Fy cm.
Complete the parallelogram (rectangle) on the two component vectors and draw its diagonal OR from O.
The diagonal OR represents the resultant force R.

written.text: Derive with the help of graph that 2aS = Vf² − Vi².
modelAnswer: From the velocity–time graph, displacement S is the area of the trapezium.
S = 1/2 (Vi + Vf)t
The slope of the velocity–time graph gives acceleration: a = (Vf − Vi)/t.
Therefore, t = (Vf − Vi)/a.
Substituting in the displacement equation: S = (Vi + Vf)(Vf − Vi)/(2a).
Multiplying both sides by 2a: 2aS = (Vf − Vi)(Vf + Vi).
Using (x − y)(x + y) = x² − y²: 2aS = Vf² − Vi².

written.text: State Pascal’s Law and Explain the working of Hydraulic Press.
modelAnswer: Pascal’s Law: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished in all directions.
A hydraulic press has a small piston of area A1 and a large piston of area A2 connected by an enclosed liquid.
A force F1 on the small piston produces pressure P = F1/A1 in the liquid.
This pressure is transmitted to the large piston, so F2/A2 = F1/A1.
Since A2 > A1, F2 > F1; therefore, the press produces a larger output force.

written.text: State Newton's Second Law of Motion and also derive its equation.
modelAnswer: Newton's Second Law: The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of that force.

For a body of constant mass m changing velocity from u to v in time t, change in momentum = mv − mu = m(v − u).
Acceleration a = (v − u)/t, so F ∝ m(v − u)/t = ma.
In SI units the proportionality constant is 1; therefore, F = ma.

written.text: Find out the relation for acceleration and tension of two bodies attached to the ends of string when one moves vertically and other moves horizontally.

written.text: Draw speed-time graph for the motion of a body. Using this graph derive second equation of motion: S = Vᵢt + 1/2 at²

written.text: Prove that: S = Vit + 1/2 at²
modelAnswer: For uniform acceleration, average velocity = (Vi + Vf)/2.
Displacement = average velocity × time.
Therefore, S = [(Vi + Vf)/2]t.
From the definition of acceleration: a = (Vf − Vi)/t.
Rearranging: Vf = Vi + at.
Substitute Vf = Vi + at into S = [(Vi + Vf)/2]t:
S = [(Vi + Vi + at)/2]t = (2Vi + at)t/2.
Therefore, S = Vit + 1/2 at^2.

written.text: State Newton's second law of motion. Derive an expression of force and hence define SI unit of force.
modelAnswer: Newton’s second law states that the force acting on a body is proportional to the rate of change of its momentum and acts in the direction of that force.
For a body of constant mass m, momentum p = mv.
Therefore, F ∝ change in momentum/time = m(v − u)/t = ma.
In SI, the proportionality constant is 1, so F = ma.
One newton (1 N) is the force that produces an acceleration of 1 m/s² in a mass of 1 kg; 1 N = 1 kg m/s².

rubric.why: Newton’s second law relates force to the rate of change of momentum.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that force is proportional to the rate of change of momentum and acts in its direction.

rubric.why: The derivation uses momentum p = mv for constant mass.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for applying p = mv and relating change in momentum to mass and change in velocity.

rubric.why: For constant mass, the rate of change of velocity is acceleration, giving the force relation.
rubric.description: Obtains the force equation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for deriving F = ma (with the proportionality constant taken as 1 in SI).

rubric.why: The SI unit follows from F = ma.
rubric.description: Defines the SI unit of force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining one newton as the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s², or stating 1 N = 1 kg m/s².

written.text: What is meant by kinetic energy? Derive its equation.
modelAnswer: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion.
The work done to bring a body from rest to speed v is its kinetic energy.
W = Fs and F = ma, so W = mas.
For a body starting from rest, v² = u² + 2as and u = 0; therefore, s = v²/(2a).
W = ma × v²/(2a) = 1/2mv².
Therefore, kinetic energy, KE = 1/2mv².

written.text: A car moving at a velocity of 30 m s⁻¹ slows down uniformly to 15 m s⁻¹ in 5 s. Find the retardation produced.

Formula: a = (v − u) / t.
Substitution: a = (15 − 30) / 5 = −15 / 5 m s⁻².
Therefore, a = −3 m s⁻².
Retardation is the magnitude of acceleration, so retardation = 3 m s⁻².

written.text: Find the magnitude and direction of force, if its x-component is 12 N and y-component is 5 N.
modelAnswer: Given: Fx = 12 N and Fy = 5 N.
Magnitude formula: F = sqrt(Fx^2 + Fy^2).
Substitution: F = sqrt(12^2 + 5^2) N = sqrt(169) N.
Therefore, F = 13 N.
Direction: θ = tan^-1(Fy/Fx) = tan^-1(5/12) ≈ 22.6° above the positive x-axis.

written.text: State Newton's second law of motion and derive its equation.
modelAnswer: Newton's second law: The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of that force.

Since p = mv, for a body of constant mass, Δp = m(v − u).
Thus, F ∝ m(v − u)/t = ma.
In SI units, the proportionality constant is 1, so F = ma.

written.text: State Law of conservation of momentum and also derive its equation.
modelAnswer: The law of conservation of momentum states that the total momentum of an isolated system remains constant, provided no external force acts on it.
Consider two bodies of masses m1 and m2 moving with initial velocities u1 and u2; after interaction, their velocities are v1 and v2.
By Newton’s third law, the mutual forces are equal and opposite: F1 = -F2.
Using force = change in momentum/time: m1(v1 - u1)/t = -m2(v2 - u2)/t.
Therefore, m1(v1 - u1) = -m2(v2 - u2); the momentum changes are equal and opposite.
Rearranging gives m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2; hence total initial momentum equals total final momentum.

written.text: Explain the working process of hydraulic press.
modelAnswer: A hydraulic press works on Pascal’s principle: pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally in all directions.
It consists of two pistons of different cross-sectional areas connected by a pipe containing an enclosed liquid.
A force F1 on the smaller piston of area A1 produces pressure P = F1/A1 in the liquid.
The same pressure acts on the larger piston, so F2/A2 = F1/A1.
Because A2 > A1, F2 > F1; the larger force can lift or press a heavy load.

written.text: State Newton’s 2nd Law of Motion. Also derive its mathematical equation.

Since a = (v − u)/t, rate of change of momentum = ma.
Therefore, F ∝ ma.
In SI units, the proportionality constant is 1; hence F = ma.

written.text: How can third equation of motion be derived graphically?
modelAnswer: The displacement is the area under the velocity-time graph.

Therefore, v² = u² + 2as.

written.text: State and prove law of Conservation of momentum.
modelAnswer: Consider two bodies of masses m₁ and m₂ with initial velocities u₁ and u₂ and final velocities v₁ and v₂.
During their interaction, the forces on them are F₁₂ and F₂₁, acting for the same time interval Δt.
By Newton’s third law, the interaction forces are equal and opposite: F₁₂ = −F₂₁.
Using force as the rate of change of momentum: (m₁v₁ − m₁u₁)/Δt = −(m₂v₂ − m₂u₂)/Δt.
Rearranging gives m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
Therefore, total initial momentum equals total final momentum. The total momentum remains constant when no external force acts.

written.text: Why a standard unit is needed to measure a quantity correctly.
modelAnswer: A standard unit provides a common basis for comparing measurements.
Standard units are universally accepted and give consistent results, avoiding confusion when measurements are recorded or communicated.
written.followUp: Why is it important to use the same standard unit when comparing measurements made by different people?

rubric.why: Checks that standard units provide a shared basis for comparing measurements.
rubric.description: Explains that a standard unit allows measurements to be compared on a common basis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the common comparison purpose of standard units.

rubric.why: Checks that standard units make measurements understandable and reliable.
rubric.description: Explains that standard units are universally accepted, avoid confusion, or give consistent results.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid benefit of using standard units.

written.text: What are distance-time graph and speed-time graph?
modelAnswer: A distance-time graph shows how distance changes with time, with distance plotted against time.
A speed-time graph shows how speed changes with time, with speed plotted against time.
written.followUp: What does the slope of a distance-time graph represent, and what does the area under a speed-time graph represent?

rubric.why: Checks the axes or quantities represented in a distance-time graph.
rubric.description: Defines a distance-time graph as distance plotted against time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct graph description.

rubric.why: Checks the axes or quantities represented in a speed-time graph.
rubric.description: Defines a speed-time graph as speed plotted against time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct graph description.

written.text: What kind of changes in motion may be produced by a force?
modelAnswer: A force may start or stop an object, or change its speed.
A force may also change the direction of an object's motion.
written.followUp: State two effects a force can have on the motion of an object.

rubric.why: Checks that a force can change an object's speed or state of motion.
rubric.description: States that a force can start or stop an object, or change its speed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct change in speed or state of motion.

rubric.why: Checks that a force can change the direction in which an object moves.
rubric.description: States that a force can change an object's direction of motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a change in direction.

written.text: State Newton’s second law of motion. Also define the unit of force.
modelAnswer: Newton’s second law states that the force acting on a body is directly proportional to the rate of change of its momentum and acts in the same direction.
For constant mass, F = ma.
The SI unit of force is the newton (N).
One newton is the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².
written.followUp: A 2 kg object accelerates at 3 m/s². Find the force acting on it and state its SI unit.

rubric.why: Checks the statement of Newton's second law or its equation for constant mass.
rubric.description: States that force is proportional to the rate of change of momentum, or gives F = ma.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the law or its equation.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of the newton in terms of mass and acceleration.
rubric.description: Defines one newton as the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct unit definition.

written.text: What are rectangular components of a vector and their values?
modelAnswer: The rectangular components of a vector are its components along two mutually perpendicular directions, usually the horizontal and vertical axes.
If a vector of magnitude A makes an angle θ with the horizontal, its horizontal component is Ax = A cos θ and its vertical component is Ay = A sin θ.
Their values depend on the magnitude of the vector and the angle it makes with the axes.
followUp
written.followUp: A vector of magnitude 10 N makes an angle of 30° with the horizontal. Find its horizontal and vertical components.

rubric.why: The vector is resolved into components along two perpendicular axes.
rubric.description: Identifies the two rectangular components and their values.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both component formulas, with the horizontal component using cosine and the vertical component using sine.

rubric.why: Rectangular components act along perpendicular directions.
rubric.description: States that the components are at right angles to each other.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the components are perpendicular or at 90°.

written.text: Define neutral equilibrium and give its two examples.
modelAnswer: A body is in neutral equilibrium if, when displaced slightly, it neither tends to return to its original position nor moves farther away; its centre of gravity remains at the same height.
Examples are a ball on a horizontal surface and a cylinder rolling on a horizontal surface.
written.followUp: What is neutral equilibrium? Give two examples of bodies in neutral equilibrium.

accept: height of centre of gravity remains unchanged
centre of gravity remains at the same height
rubric.why: In neutral equilibrium, a small displacement does not change the height of the centre of gravity.
rubric.description: Defines neutral equilibrium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that after displacement the body neither returns nor moves farther away, or that its centre of gravity remains at the same height.

rubric.why: These are standard examples of neutral equilibrium.
rubric.description: Gives two examples.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two valid examples, such as a ball on a horizontal surface and a cylinder rolling on a horizontal surface.

written.text: A slow-moving car may have more kinetic energy than a fast-moving motorcycle. How is this possible?
modelAnswer: Kinetic energy is given by KE = ½mv², so it depends on mass as well as the square of speed.
A car has much greater mass than a motorcycle; therefore, even at a lower speed, its kinetic energy may be greater.
written.followUp: A truck and a car move at the same speed. Which has greater kinetic energy, and why?

rubric.why: Kinetic energy depends on both mass and the square of speed.
rubric.description: Uses the kinetic-energy relationship.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that kinetic energy is proportional to mass and the square of speed, or writing the formula.

rubric.why: A car has much greater mass than a motorcycle, which can outweigh the motorcycle's speed advantage.
rubric.description: Explains how the slow-moving car can have more kinetic energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the car's much larger mass can give it greater kinetic energy despite its lower speed.

written.text: Distinguish between force and pressure.
modelAnswer: Force is a push or pull that can change or tend to change the state of motion or shape of a body.
Pressure is the normal force acting per unit area of a surface: P = F/A.
Force is measured in newtons, whereas pressure is measured in pascals (N/m²).
written.followUp: Define pressure and write its SI unit. How is pressure related to force and area?

rubric.why: Force is described as a push or pull acting on a body.
rubric.description: Defines force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying force as a push or pull.

rubric.why: Pressure is the normal force acting per unit area of a surface.
rubric.description: Defines pressure in a way that distinguishes it from force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that pressure is force per unit area.

written.text: State the basic principle used in the hydraulic brake system of the automobile.
modelAnswer: The hydraulic brake system works on Pascal’s principle: pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted undiminished in all directions.
The pressure is transmitted through the brake fluid to the pistons at the wheels, forcing the brake shoes or pads against the wheels.
written.followUp: State Pascal’s principle and describe how it helps a hydraulic lift raise a heavy load.

rubric.why: This is the principle on which hydraulic brakes operate.
rubric.description: States Pascal’s principle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted undiminished in all directions.

rubric.why: The transmitted pressure operates the brake pistons and applies the brakes.
rubric.description: Connects the principle to the automobile brake system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that pressure in the liquid is transmitted to the brake pistons, which press the brake shoes or pads against the wheel.

written.text: State the main scales used for the measurement of temperature.
modelAnswer: The main temperature scales are Celsius (centigrade), Fahrenheit and Kelvin.
Kelvin is the SI scale of temperature.
written.followUp: Name the SI temperature scale and state the freezing point of water on it.

rubric.why: Celsius and Fahrenheit are commonly used temperature scales.
rubric.description: Names the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming Celsius and Fahrenheit.

rubric.why: Kelvin is the SI temperature scale.
rubric.description: Names the Kelvin scale.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming Kelvin.

written.text: Define magnetic field of a magnet.
modelAnswer: The magnetic field of a magnet is the region around it in which its magnetic force can be experienced.
written.followUp: Define the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire.

rubric.why: Checks identification of where the magnetic field exists.
rubric.description: States that the field is the region or space around a magnet.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the region around the magnet.

rubric.why: Checks the defining effect of a magnetic field.
rubric.description: States that magnetic force can be experienced or detected there.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the magnetic force in that region.

written.text: Write any one method for demagnetization of a magnet.
modelAnswer: Place the magnet inside a solenoid connected to an alternating-current supply.
Slowly withdraw the magnet from the solenoid while the current is flowing.
written.followUp: Describe how a magnet can be demagnetized by heating.

rubric.why: Checks identification of a valid demagnetization method.
rubric.description: Names a valid method, such as heating, hammering, or using an alternating-current solenoid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming one valid method.

rubric.why: Checks the essential procedure when using an AC solenoid or heating.
rubric.description: For the AC method, places the magnet in a solenoid carrying alternating current and slowly withdraws it; alternatively, states that the magnet is heated strongly or hammered repeatedly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid method described with its essential action.

Form a hypothesis and make deductions from it.
Test the deductions by experimentation.
Record and analyse the results; draw a conclusion.
written.followUp: Write the main steps of the scientific method and explain why experiments are performed.

rubric.why: Checks the starting stage of scientific investigation.
rubric.description: Includes observation or identification of a problem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for observation or identifying a problem.

rubric.why: Checks knowledge of the remaining scientific-method stages.
rubric.description: Includes stages such as forming a hypothesis, making deductions, experimentation, and obtaining results.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming at least two relevant further stages.

written.text: Distinguish between a theory and a law of Physics?
modelAnswer: A law of Physics describes a regular relationship or states what happens in nature.
A theory of Physics explains why or how the observed phenomena occur.
written.followUp: State one difference between a scientific hypothesis and a theory.

rubric.why: Checks what a physical law states.
rubric.description: Explains that a law describes a consistent relationship or what happens in nature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the descriptive role of a law.

rubric.why: Checks the explanatory role of a theory.
rubric.description: Explains that a theory explains why or how natural phenomena occur.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the explanatory role of a theory.

written.text: Define momentum and express Newton’s 2nd law of motion in terms of change in momentum.
modelAnswer: Momentum is the product of the mass of a body and its velocity: p = mv.
Newton’s second law states that the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force.
The change in momentum takes place in the direction of the applied force.
For a change in momentum during a time interval, F = change in momentum / time.
written.followUp: A force acts on a 3 kg body and changes its velocity from 2 m/s to 6 m/s in 4 s. Find the change in momentum and the force.

rubric.why: Checks the definition and expression for momentum.
rubric.description: Defines momentum as the product of mass and velocity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that momentum equals mass times velocity.

rubric.why: Checks the rate-of-change statement in Newton’s second law.
rubric.description: States that the rate of change of momentum is directly proportional to the applied force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the proportionality between force and rate of change of momentum.

rubric.why: Checks the direction specified by Newton’s second law.
rubric.description: States that the change in momentum takes place in the direction of the applied force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the direction relationship.

rubric.why: Checks the mathematical expression of the law.
rubric.description: Expresses force as the change in momentum divided by the time taken.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct force–momentum equation.

written.text: A ball is dropped from the top of a tower. The ball reaches the ground in 5 s. Find the height of the tower and the velocity of the ball with which it strikes the ground.
modelAnswer: Given: u = 0 m/s, t = 5 s, g = 9.8 m/s².
Height: s = ut + ½gt².
Velocity on striking the ground: v = u + gt.
v = 0 m/s + (9.8 m/s²)(5 s) = 49 m/s downward.
written.followUp: A stone is dropped from rest and reaches the ground in 4 s. Find the height fallen and its velocity on reaching the ground. Take g = 9.8 m/s².

rubric.why: Checks correct extraction of the given data and initial condition.
rubric.description: Identifies u = 0 m/s, t = 5 s, and g = 9.8 m/s².
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating the dropped-from-rest condition and the given values.

rubric.why: Checks the displacement equation and the calculated tower height.
rubric.description: Uses s = ut + ½gt² and obtains the height as 122.5 m.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct equation/substitution and 1 mark for the correct height with unit.

rubric.why: Checks the velocity equation and the calculated impact velocity.
rubric.description: Uses v = u + gt and obtains 49 m/s downward.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct equation/substitution and 1 mark for the correct velocity with direction.

written.text: State the law of conservation of energy. Explain it with the help of an example of a body falling from certain height in terms of its potential energy and kinetic energy.
modelAnswer: The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form into another.
At a certain height, a body has maximum potential energy and zero kinetic energy if it is at rest.
As the body falls, its potential energy decreases and is converted into kinetic energy, which increases.
Just before reaching the ground, its kinetic energy is maximum and its potential energy is minimum; the total mechanical energy remains constant if air resistance is neglected.
written.followUp: State the law of conservation of energy and explain how energy changes as a ball is thrown vertically upward.

rubric.why: This states the conservation law and the transformation of energy.
rubric.description: States that energy is neither created nor destroyed, but changes from one form to another.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the law of conservation of energy, including the idea that energy is transformed rather than lost or created.

rubric.why: At the starting height, the falling body has gravitational potential energy and is momentarily at rest.
rubric.description: Identifies the body's energy at the start of the fall as potential energy, with zero or negligible kinetic energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing the body's energy at the initial height.

rubric.why: During the fall, gravitational potential energy is converted into kinetic energy.
rubric.description: Explains that potential energy decreases while kinetic energy increases as the body falls.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the energy changes during the fall.

rubric.why: The sum of potential and kinetic energy remains constant, assuming air resistance is neglected.
rubric.description: States that total energy remains constant and/or that kinetic energy is greatest at the ground.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for concluding that total mechanical energy is conserved, or correctly describing the energy at ground level.

written.text: Calculate the pressure of column of mercury 76 cm high. Density of mercury is 13.6×10³ kg m⁻³.
modelAnswer: Given: h = 76 cm = 0.76 m, ρ = 13.6 × 10³ kg m⁻³, g = 9.8 m s⁻².
Formula: p = ρgh.
Substitution: p = (13.6 × 10³ kg m⁻³)(9.8 m s⁻²)(0.76 m).
Calculation: p = 101292.8 kg m⁻¹ s⁻².
Answer: p ≈ 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa.
written.followUp: Calculate the pressure exerted by a 50 cm column of water. Take the density of water as 1000 kg m⁻³ and g = 9.8 m s⁻².

rubric.why: The height is converted to SI units before substitution.
rubric.description: Converts the column height to 0.76 m.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct SI height.

rubric.why: This is the relation for pressure due to a liquid column.
rubric.description: Uses p = ρgh.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula.

rubric.why: The given values are correctly substituted into the formula.
rubric.description: Substitutes the density, gravitational acceleration, and height.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct substitution using SI values.

rubric.why: The calculation gives the pressure exerted by the mercury column.
rubric.description: Calculates the pressure as approximately 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either equivalent numerical result.

rubric.why: Pressure is expressed in pascals in SI units.
rubric.description: Gives the answer with the correct unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Pa.

written.text: The temperature of a normal human body on Fahrenheit scale is 98.6°F. Convert it into Celsius scale and Kelvin scale.
modelAnswer: Given: T_F = 98.6°F.
Formula: T_C = 5/9(T_F − 32).
Formula: T_K = T_C + 273.
Substitution and answer: T_K = 37 + 273 = 310 K.
written.followUp: The temperature of a liquid is 68°F. Convert it into Celsius and Kelvin scales.

rubric.why: The Fahrenheit-to-Celsius relation is needed for the conversion.
rubric.description: States or correctly applies the relation °C = 5/9(°F − 32).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct conversion formula or its correct application.

rubric.why: Correct substitution uses the given Fahrenheit temperature.
rubric.description: Substitutes 98.6°F into the Celsius conversion formula.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correct substitution.

rubric.why: The Fahrenheit temperature converts to 37°C.
rubric.description: Finds the temperature in Celsius.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 37°C.

rubric.why: Kelvin temperature is found by adding 273 to the Celsius temperature at this level.
rubric.description: Uses the relation K = °C + 273 and substitutes the Celsius value.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct Kelvin conversion relation and substitution.

rubric.why: Adding 273 to 37°C gives 310 K; using 273.15 gives 310.15 K.
rubric.description: Gives the temperature in Kelvin with the correct unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 310 K (or 310.15 K when 273.15 is used).
